title: Rome vs Carthage: The ENTIRE War From Both Sides
sources: World History Encyclopedia, First Punic War: https://www.worldhistory.org/First_Punic_War/
World History Encyclopedia, Third Punic War: https://worldhistory.org/Third_Punic_War
History Revealed, How many elephants did Hannibal take over the Alps?: https://www.historyrevealed.com/eras/ancient-rome/how-many-elephants-did-hannibal-take-over-the-alps/
Dickinson College Commentaries, Chronology of Hannibal's life: https://dcc.dickinson.edu/node/240
Plutarch, Life of Cato the Elder 26-27 (Perseus): https://cts.perseids.org/read/greekLit/tlg0007/tlg025/perseus-eng2/25.1-27.2
The Death of Carthage, Scipio Aemilianus destroys Carthage (Polybius XXXIX): https://thedeathofcarthage.com/1752/publius-cornelius-scipio-aemilianus-destroys-carthage/

beats.say: Spring, 146 BC. The greatest city in Africa is burning, and it has been burning for days.
Its people fought the Romans street by street, for seven days. Now about fifty thousand survivors walk out of the ruins. Every one of them will be sold as a slave.
And the Roman general who ordered all of it is standing on a hill, watching. And he is crying.

This is the end of Rome versus Carthage. The war of Hannibal, and his elephants over the Alps. The Punic Wars, 264 to 146 BC. Three wars, one hundred and eighteen years, and two of the most powerful cities in the ancient world.

card.text: Rome vs Carthage: the Punic Wars

beats.say: The Romans wrote almost everything we know about it. So today we tell it from both sides, and we ask a hard question. Did Carthage have to die?
Let's start with the side that lost, because that's the side you rarely hear. Carthage sat on the coast of North Africa, in what is now Tunisia.

scene.caption: The Punic harbours of Carthage, today

beats.say: It was founded around 814 BC by settlers from Tyre, a Phoenician city on the coast of what is now Lebanon. Legend says its founder was a queen called Dido.

The legend also says the locals offered her as much land as an ox hide could cover. So she cut the hide into thin strips, and claimed an entire hill. Carthage started the way it would live. As a city of very clever traders.

talk.text: As much land as an ox hide covers?
Fetch me a very sharp knife.

beats.say: By the 200s BC, Carthage was the richest power in the western Mediterranean. It had colonies along the African coast, in Spain, on Sardinia, and on the western half of Sicily. And it had the best navy around.

Now the other side. Rome was a farming republic in Italy. By about 275 BC, it had made itself master of almost the whole peninsula. It had a huge army of citizen farmers. What it did not have was a single serious warship.

talk.text: You stay on land. We keep the sea.

beats.say: Between them lay Sicily, and on its northeastern tip, a town called Messana. And in Messana lived the Mamertines.
The Mamertines were mercenaries from southern Italy who had seized the town for themselves. When the king of Syracuse came to crush them, they called for help. First from Carthage. Then from Rome.

talk.text: Write to Carthage. Ask for help.
And write to Rome as well.

beats.say: This was a terrible idea. Two great powers, both invited into the same small town, by the same people, who were loyal to nobody.

Rome sent a consul with two legions, about sixteen thousand men. He crossed the narrow strait and took Messana. Carthage saw an Italian army standing on its doorstep. Rome saw a Carthaginian empire one short crossing from Italy.

card.note: World History Encyclopedia, First Punic War

beats.say: Both sides believed they were defending themselves. Both sides were partly right. And so began a war over a town that neither of them had owned.
Nobody expected it to last a generation. It would last twenty three years.
On land, Rome won quickly. But Sicily is an island, and Carthage ruled the sea around it. Every town Rome took could be supplied by Carthaginian ships. Rome needed a navy. It had none.
So in 260 BC, Rome did something wild. It built a fleet of about a hundred and twenty warships, in sixty days.

card.note: World History Encyclopedia, First Punic War

beats.say: A hundred and twenty ships in sixty days. That is two warships, every single day, for two months.
They probably copied Carthaginian ships they had captured. And while the ships were still being built, the rowers practised on wooden benches, on dry land.

talk.text: When do we get a sea?
When the ship is finished. Row.

beats.say: Then they added a trick. A long boarding bridge, about eleven metres, with an iron spike on the end. The Romans called it the corvus, the raven. Drop it onto an enemy deck, and the spike holds it there. Now a sea battle becomes a land battle. And land battles were what Rome did best.

scene.caption: The corvus: a Roman boarding bridge

talk.text: What's that thing on the front?

beats.say: At Mylae, off the north coast of Sicily, the brand new Roman navy met the Carthaginians, and won.
Rome got bold. In 256 BC, it beat Carthage again at sea, at Ecnomus, and landed an army in Africa itself, under a consul called Regulus. Carthage had never been so close to losing.
So Carthage hired a Greek soldier called Xanthippus. He used cavalry and a hundred war elephants, and in 255 BC he crushed Regulus near Tunis. About twelve thousand Romans died.

talk.text: We need a general who has beaten Romans.

beats.say: Then the sea itself joined the war. The Roman fleet that rescued the survivors sailed into a storm. Ancient writers say as many as a hundred thousand men drowned. More storms followed. Rome lost whole fleets to the weather, without a single enemy in sight.

And then there is the admiral Claudius Pulcher. Before his attack at Drepana, the priests reported that the sacred chickens would not eat. A very bad omen. So, the story goes, Pulcher threw the chickens into the sea, and said that if they would not eat, they could drink.

card.text: If they won't eat, let them drink.

scene.caption: Claudius Pulcher and the sacred chickens

beats.say: He lost ninety three of his hundred and twenty ships.
Ninety three out of a hundred and twenty. Nearly four ships in every five.

Meanwhile, Carthage found a real commander. Hamilcar, nicknamed Barca, which probably means lightning. From a mountain base at Eryx, he fought a raiding war in Sicily that Rome could never quite finish.
But a war at sea eats money, and ships, and men. After twenty years, both cities were exhausted. Rome built one more fleet, of about two hundred warships.

On the tenth of March, 241 BC, off the Aegates Islands, that last Roman fleet caught a Carthaginian supply fleet. About fifty Carthaginian ships were sunk, seventy captured, and ten thousand men taken prisoner.

card.note: World History Encyclopedia, First Punic War

beats.say: Hamilcar's men were still holding out on their mountain. But Carthage told him to make peace.
The price of peace was high. Carthage left Sicily, and paid three thousand two hundred talents of silver over ten years. Sicily became Rome's first province outside Italy.
Three thousand two hundred talents over ten years. Three hundred and twenty talents of silver, every year, for a decade.
Then Carthage could not pay its own mercenaries. They rebelled, and Carthage spent years fighting its own army in Africa. Hamilcar led the side that saved the city.

talk.text: Rome has it. Well, it will have.

beats.say: And while Carthage was busy, the mercenaries on Sardinia offered the island to Rome. Rome took it. When Carthage protested, Rome declared war, and only stopped when Carthage handed over Sardinia and Corsica, and paid even more silver.

talk.text: That island wasn't in the treaty!

beats.say: From the Carthaginian side, it proved something. A treaty with Rome only lasted as long as Rome wanted it to.
So Hamilcar looked west, to Spain. Spain had silver mines, and men to recruit. If Carthage could not have Sicily, it would build a new empire there.
Before he sailed, he made a sacrifice at the altar. The Greek historian Polybius tells what happened next. Hamilcar's son, about nine years old, begged to come along.
His father agreed, on one condition. The boy put his hand on the altar, and swore that he would never be a friend to Rome. The boy's name was Hannibal.

card.text: Never be a friend to Rome.
card.who: Hannibal's oath, as told by Polybius

scene.header: Hannibal's oath, as told by Polybius

talk.text: Put your hand on the altar.
I swear I will never be a friend to Rome.

beats.say: Hamilcar died in Spain in 229 BC. His son-in-law, Hasdrubal, took over, and signed a deal with Rome. Carthage would stay south of the river Ebro.

talk.text: You stay south of the Ebro.
And you stay north of it.

beats.say: In 221 BC, Hasdrubal was murdered, and the army chose Hannibal as its general. He was about twenty five. Two years later, he attacked Saguntum, a town south of the Ebro, but a friend of Rome.
Was this an attack on Rome? Carthage said no. Saguntum was on Carthage's side of the line. Rome said yes. Saguntum was Rome's friend. Historians still argue about it.
Rome sent envoys to Carthage, and demanded that Hannibal be handed over. The Carthaginian council refused. And so Rome declared war again. This time, Hannibal would not wait for Rome to come to him.
Rome planned a normal war. One army to Spain, one army to Africa. It owned the sea now, so it assumed the fighting would happen far away from Italy.
Hannibal planned something else. If he could not cross the sea, he would walk. Out of Spain, over the Pyrenees, across Gaul, over the Alps, and into Italy from the north.

scene.caption: Snow Storm: Hannibal and his Army Crossing the Alps (Turner, 1812)

talk.text: They're guarding the sea. So we take the mountains.
Nobody marches an army over the Alps.

beats.say: He did not go light. Writers give his army on the road as tens of thousands of men, thousands of horses, and about thirty seven war elephants. When he reached the Alps, he had about fifty thousand foot soldiers and nine thousand cavalry.
He reached the mountains in late September or early October. Far too late in the year. Snow was already falling on the high passes.
Mountain tribes rolled rocks down onto the column. Horses and pack animals slipped off the narrow paths and fell. And the elephants, animals from the warm south, had to be walked through ice.

talk.text: It is from Africa. It has never seen snow.

beats.say: Livy says the crossing took sixteen days. Exactly which pass he used is still argued about, more than two thousand two hundred years later. One recent study points to a high pass on today's border between France and Italy.
When he came down into the plains of northern Italy, he had about twenty six thousand men left. He had lost more than half his army, before fighting a single Roman battle.
About fifty nine thousand men and horsemen went up. About twenty six thousand came down. Fewer than one in two made it.
Now the other side. In Rome, they could hardly believe it. The war they had planned to fight in Spain and Africa was suddenly in Italy.
A Roman army rushed north to meet him. At the river Trebia, in December, Hannibal beat it.
Most of his elephants soon died. One popular account says only a single elephant survived. But the Celtic tribes of northern Italy, who hated Rome, began joining him by the thousand.

talk.text: You came over the mountains? To fight Rome?
Then we are coming with you.

beats.say: He had crossed the Alps to break Rome's alliance. Would Rome's friends switch sides? That was the question the whole war now hung on.

chapters.title: The Worst Day in Roman History

beats.say: Summer, 217 BC. The consul Flaminius chased Hannibal south, along the shore of Lake Trasimene. Early in the morning, a thick fog rose off the water.
Hannibal's whole army was waiting in the hills above the road. The Romans marched into the fog, between the hills and the lake. And the hills attacked.
At least fifteen thousand Romans were killed. Flaminius died with them.
Rome panicked, and did something it did only in emergencies. It appointed a dictator, an old senator called Fabius Maximus. His plan was simple, and very unpopular. Don't fight.
Fabius followed Hannibal everywhere, picked off his foragers, and refused every battle. The Romans called him the Delayer, and they did not mean it as a compliment. Later they did.

talk.text: We have the biggest army in Italy. Why are we hiding?
Because he wants a battle. So he doesn't get one.

beats.say: The next year, Rome lost patience, and raised a huge army. More than eighty thousand men, under two consuls, Paullus and Varro. They found Hannibal at Cannae, in the south east of Italy.

Hannibal had fewer than fifty thousand. So he did something that generals still study today. He put his weakest troops in the centre, bulging forward, and his best African veterans hidden on both wings.

talk.text: You put us in the middle?

beats.say: The Roman legions pushed the centre back. It bent, but it didn't break. The Romans poured into the gap, deeper and deeper. Then the veterans on the wings turned inward. And Hannibal's cavalry came round behind them.
The Roman army was surrounded on every side, and packed so tightly that many men could not even raise their swords.
Nobody knows exactly how many died that afternoon. Modern estimates run from about forty four thousand to more than sixty five thousand Romans. Hannibal lost about six thousand.

scene.caption: The Death of Paulus Aemilius at Cannae (Trumbull, 1773)

beats.say: Even the lowest estimate is more than seven Romans killed for every man Hannibal lost.

scene.place: ROMAN DEATHS FOR EACH OF HANNIBAL'S

beats.say: It was one of the bloodiest single days of fighting in history.

At a nearby town called Canusium, some young Roman officers who had survived talked about giving up, and leaving Italy. One of them, a twenty year old, burst into the room, and made them all swear an oath to stay and fight. His name was Scipio. Remember him.

talk.text: Italy is lost. We should sail away.
Swear you will not abandon Rome. All of you. Swear it.

beats.say: After Cannae, the plan seemed to work. Capua, a great city in the south, opened its gates to Hannibal. Much of southern Italy switched sides.
By any normal rule of war, Rome should now ask for terms. Every other state Hannibal had ever heard of would have.
Rome did not ask. It kept raising new legions. By 213 BC it had over two hundred thousand men under arms.
Two hundred thousand men under arms, three years after Cannae. Two and a half times the whole army Rome took to Cannae.

talk.text: I've beaten you three times. Make peace.

beats.say: Now the other side. Hannibal needed siege engines, and fresh men. He asked Carthage for help. Carthage refused to send what he asked for. Historians still argue why.

talk.text: He wants more men. And siege engines.
He keeps winning. Why does he need anything?

beats.say: In 211 BC, Hannibal marched right up to the walls of Rome itself, hoping to pull the Romans away from Capua. Rome barely moved. He could not take the city, and Capua fell.
That same year, in Spain, two Roman generals were killed. They were Scipio's father, and Scipio's uncle. Rome's whole Spanish war collapsed.
Nobody wanted the Spanish command. So Rome gave it to the son. He was twenty four, and not even old enough for the post. He was elected anyway.
Scipio had studied Hannibal. In his very first campaign, he struck straight at New Carthage, Carthage's main base in Spain, and took it in a week. Then he drove Carthage out of Spain altogether.
One Carthaginian army did escape. Hannibal's brother Hasdrubal crossed the Alps too, bringing reinforcements. But at the river Metaurus, the Romans caught him, and killed him.
Then they cut off his head, carried it south, and threw it into Hannibal's camp. That is how Hannibal learned his brother was dead.

talk.text: Something was thrown over the wall, sir.

beats.say: In 204 BC, Scipio did what Regulus had tried fifty years earlier. He landed in Africa. And Carthage called Hannibal home. He had fought in Italy for fifteen years. He had won battle after battle. And he had not won the war.
Two armies, deep in North Africa, south west of Carthage. On one side, Hannibal. On the other, the young man who swore an oath after Cannae. Scipio.
Before the battle, the two generals met face to face. Hannibal offered peace. Scipio said no.

talk.text: Fortune changes. I have seen it change on me. Let us make peace.
Then let's see which way it changes today.

beats.say: Each side had around forty thousand men. But Hannibal's were mixed. Only about twelve to fifteen thousand were his old veterans. And for once, the Romans had the stronger cavalry.
That cavalry belonged to Masinissa, a Numidian prince who had joined Scipio. Keep an eye on him. He matters later.

talk.text: Our prince rides with Rome now.

beats.say: Hannibal opened with eighty war elephants. But they were badly trained, and they scattered. Some panicked and turned back onto Hannibal's own men.

talk.text: Open the lines! Let them through!

beats.say: Then Masinissa's horsemen chased off Hannibal's cavalry, and came back to hit his infantry from behind. It was Cannae, in reverse.
About twenty thousand Carthaginians died, and about twenty thousand more were captured. Rome lost around fifteen hundred.
About twenty thousand Carthaginians killed, against about fifteen hundred Romans. More than thirteen for one. The numbers of Cannae, turned round.
Hannibal escaped. He would never command a Carthaginian army again. And Carthage asked for peace.

The terms were brutal. Carthage gave up Spain. It handed over almost all its warships, and at least a hundred of them were burned in the harbour. And it would pay ten thousand talents of silver, spread over fifty years.
Ten thousand talents over fifty years. Two hundred talents a year. Payments that would outlive almost everyone who signed the treaty.
Fifty years. That number is important. Rome had built a timer into the treaty, and nobody yet knew what would happen when it ran out.
Scipio went home a hero, with a new name. Africanus.
You might expect Hannibal's story to end at Zama. It doesn't. In 196 BC, Carthage elected him to its highest office, one of its two chief magistrates.
And the general turned out to be a very good accountant. His reforms put the city's money in order, and made the huge payments to Rome easy to afford.

talk.text: Where did all this money come from?

beats.say: This was good news for Carthage. And it worried people in Rome a great deal. A defeated city that pays its bills on time is a city that is recovering.
Rome grew suspicious. And in 195 BC, Hannibal ran. First to Tyre, the city Carthage had come from. Then to the court of Antiochus, the great king of the east.
He spent the rest of his life moving from court to court, advising kings who were at war with Rome. He even commanded a fleet, and lost. Rome kept beating every king who took him in.

talk.text: Rome is coming. I'd move fast, Your Majesty.
Hannibal is there? Then we are coming.

beats.say: Finally, in Bithynia, in what is now Turkey, the Romans closed in. Rather than be captured, Hannibal took poison. He was about sixty five.
Ancient writers give him one last line.

card.text: Let us put an end to this life, which has caused so much dread to the Romans.

lines: Let us put an end to this life,
which has caused so much dread

beats.say: And Scipio Africanus? The man who saved Rome never held real power there again. His rivals attacked him with lawsuits, and he went into bitter retirement. He died around the same time as Hannibal.
The two greatest generals of the age. Both pushed out by their own cities. Both dead within a few years of each other.
And Carthage, without either of them, kept paying. Year after year. Until the last payment came due.
In 153 BC, an old Roman senator called Cato visited Carthage. What he saw alarmed him. Carthage was paying Rome regularly, and it had recovered.
Back in the Senate, Plutarch says, Cato dropped a fresh fig from Africa onto the floor. Then he reminded the senators that the land where it grew was only three days' sail from Rome.
And after that, whatever the Senate was voting on, Cato added the same line at the end.

card.text: In my opinion, Carthage must be destroyed.
card.who: Cato the Elder, as told by Plutarch

scene.header: Cato the Elder, as told by Plutarch

talk.text: Cato, this is a vote about drains.

beats.say: Not everyone agreed. Another senator, Scipio Nasica, ended every vote the opposite way. Carthage must be spared. Rome argued with itself about it for years.

talk.text: Can we vote on the drains now?

beats.say: Meanwhile, remember Masinissa, the Numidian horseman from Zama? He was now an old king, and Rome's friend. He kept taking Carthaginian land, piece by piece. And since the last war, Carthage was not free to fight its own wars.
By 150 BC, Masinissa had taken about half the land Carthage held. So Carthage finally raised its own army, and fought him. And lost.
For Rome, it was the excuse it had been waiting for. Carthage had gone to war without permission.
Carthage begged for peace and offered to obey. Rome asked for three hundred noble children as hostages. Carthage sent them. Rome asked for every weapon in the city. Carthage handed them over.
Then Rome made its final demand. Leave the city, and settle at least sixteen kilometres from the sea.
Sixteen kilometres. About a four hour walk from the sea, for a city that lived on ships.
For a city of sailors and traders, that meant death anyway. Carthage, with no weapons left, refused.
And the city got ready to fight anyway. It sent fire-ships against the Roman fleet, and raided the Roman siege engines. Against an army of up to eighty thousand, Carthage held out for three years.
In 147 BC, Rome sent a new commander. Scipio Aemilianus. In the spring of 146 BC, his men broke into the city. Seven days of street fighting followed, house by house.

About fifty thousand people finally came out and surrendered. All of them were sold into slavery. Hasdrubal, the last Carthaginian general, surrendered too. His wife did not. Ancient writers say she threw herself and her two children into the flames.

And Scipio Aemilianus wept. The historian Polybius was standing next to him. Scipio quoted a line from Homer about the fall of Troy, and told Polybius he was afraid that one day, someone would give the same order about Rome.

card.text: Someday this may also be the fate of Rome.
card.who: Scipio Aemilianus, as told by Polybius

scene.header: Scipio Aemilianus, as told by Polybius

talk.text: You have won. Why are you crying?
One day, someone will give the same order about Rome.

beats.say: You may have heard that the Romans then salted the earth, so nothing would grow. That part is a later invention. They didn't need salt. They had already done enough.
Carthage's land became a Roman province, called Africa. Towns that had sided with Rome, like Utica, were rewarded and freed from tax.
Rome had begun the Punic Wars as a power in Italy. It ended them as the master of the western Mediterranean.
So which side was right? Rome would say it fought for its own survival. It had been invaded, and nearly destroyed, by a man who swore as a boy to be its enemy.
Carthage would say it kept every treaty, paid every talent, and was destroyed anyway. Its first war began over a town it did not own. Its last war began because it defended itself.
Notice what both answers share. Each side believed it was defending itself. That belief is how most wars begin, and how this one lasted so long.

And the strange thing is, we only hear Carthage's side through its enemies. Almost nothing Carthage wrote about itself survived. Almost every word we have about Hannibal was written by Greeks and Romans.
Think of the people, too. Farmers, sailors and shopkeepers on both sides paid for choices made in council chambers. The ones who fought street by street in Carthage were not senators.
Perhaps that is the real lesson of the Punic Wars. Fear drove both cities. Rome feared a rival it could not control. Carthage feared a neighbour it could not trust.
Even so, the Romans could not make him a simple villain. Their own writers made him the most dangerous, and the most admired, enemy Rome ever had.
Today, the ruins of Carthage lie beside the sea, next to Tunis.

So hold on to that, as you watch other borders in other stories. Two sides. One line on a map. And each one certain that the line was drawn against it. We will keep asking, every time, who really started it.

Two cities fought for a hundred and eighteen years over who would rule the sea between them. One won everything. The other is remembered mostly through the words of the people who destroyed it. That is the cost of a history written by the winner, and it is why we ask both sides.

talk.text: You stay on land. We keep the sea.

outro.text: Every border has two sides. Carthage lost the war, and then lost the right to tell its own story.
outro.question: Was Rome defending itself, or was Carthage already beaten?

hook: In 146 BC, Rome burned Carthage to the ground. It had taken three wars and 118 years.
about: Rome vs Carthage, the Punic Wars (264–146 BC), told from both sides: the fight over Sicily, Rome building a navy in sixty days, Hamilcar and the boy who swore never to be Rome's friend, Hannibal crossing the Alps, Trasimene and Cannae, Scipio and Zama, Hannibal's exile, Cato's fig, and the destruction of Carthage.

de.title: Rom gegen Karthago: Der GESAMTE Krieg von beiden Seiten
de.description:
146 v. Chr. brannte Rom Karthago nieder. Es hatte drei Kriege und 118 Jahre gedauert.

Die Punischen Kriege (264–146 v. Chr.), erzählt von beiden Seiten: der Streit um Sizilien, Roms Flotte in sechzig Tagen, Hamilkar und der Junge, der schwor, niemals Roms Freund zu sein, Hannibals Zug über die Alpen, Trasimener See und Cannae, Scipio und Zama, Hannibals Exil, Catos Feige und die Zerstörung Karthagos.

es.title: Roma contra Cartago: TODA la guerra desde ambos lados
es.description:
En el 146 a. C., Roma arrasó Cartago. Le había costado tres guerras y 118 años.

Las guerras púnicas (264–146 a. C.) contadas desde ambos lados: la lucha por Sicilia, la flota romana construida en sesenta días, Amílcar y el niño que juró no ser nunca amigo de Roma, Aníbal cruzando los Alpes, Trasimeno y Cannas, Escipión y Zama, el exilio de Aníbal, el higo de Catón y la destrucción de Cartago.

fr.title: Rome contre Carthage : TOUTE la guerre des deux côtés
fr.description:
En 146 av. J.-C., Rome rasa Carthage. Il lui avait fallu trois guerres et 118 ans.

Les guerres puniques (264–146 av. J.-C.) racontées des deux côtés : la lutte pour la Sicile, la flotte romaine construite en soixante jours, Hamilcar et l'enfant qui jura de ne jamais être l'ami de Rome, Hannibal franchissant les Alpes, Trasimène et Cannes, Scipion et Zama, l'exil d'Hannibal, la figue de Caton et la destruction de Carthage.

pt.title: Roma contra Cartago: a guerra INTEIRA dos dois lados
pt.description:
Em 146 a.C., Roma arrasou Cartago. Foram precisas três guerras e 118 anos.

As Guerras Púnicas (264–146 a.C.) contadas dos dois lados: a disputa pela Sicília, a frota romana construída em sessenta dias, Amílcar e o menino que jurou nunca ser amigo de Roma, Aníbal atravessando os Alpes, Trasimeno e Canas, Cipião e Zama, o exílio de Aníbal, o figo de Catão e a destruição de Cartago.
